models.best: Inferred from its principle that gifts create obligations and trust, so local papers and community broadcasts are shared among members who return the favour, and voices gain standing without an advertising market. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that favours are returned, so airtime, columns and ownership of papers pass among kin and allies, while outsiders have no route into print or on air. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Mauss, The Gift

models.best: Inferred from its principle that a household plans its work around its own needs, so a family-run local paper or radio station can serve farm households at modest cost, without a push for profit. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that production serves household consumption, so a family-run paper or station closes when household labour and cash run short, and rural areas are left with little news. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Chayanov, The Theory of Peasant Economy

models.best: Inferred from its principle that a central store collects revenue and redistributes it, so public broadcasting can be paid from common revenue and reach every household, not only those who can pay. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that the centre allocates what it collects, so licences, airtime and printing rights go to officials and favoured households, and the broadcaster answers to whoever controls the store. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Polanyi, The Great Transformation

models.best: Inferred from its principle that trade income pays for printing houses and news for merchants, so commercial papers are run efficiently for the trade and for the owners who profit from it. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that labour is extracted through the ownership of people, so enslaved people are denied any schooling or access to print, and the press speaks only for owners. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Williams, Capitalism and Slavery

models.best: Inferred from its principle that lords and the Church protect and fund scribes in return for service, so records, letters and local news are kept within each manor for local justice. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that services are owed to a lord, so tenants' speech and news are bound to the manor's court, and no free press exists to check the lord's account of events. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Bloch, Feudal Society

models.best: Inferred from its principle that guild statutes fix training and quality, so printers and booksellers keep a common standard, and buyers can rely on what they buy. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that masters control entry under statute, so new printers and publishers wait for places, and a closed body decides which titles and papers may appear. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Epstein, Freedom and Growth

models.best: Inferred from its principle that the state seeks a trade surplus and national strength, so it funds printing and news that serve trade and state power, and licenses them to that end. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that the state regulates trade and production toward national gain, so presses are licensed, news is steered toward state goals, and printing that criticises trade policy is restricted. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Heckscher, Mercantilism

models.best: Inferred from its principle that only agriculture makes a net product, so a tax on land funds public reporting on farming, grain and rural markets, the sectors the model treats as the source of wealth. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that a single tax on land funds the state, so public money for general news and broadcasting stays thin, and only farming and grain information is well served. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Meek, The Economics of Physiocracy

models.best: The case Newspaper ownership concentration and content variety found that greater ownership concentration went with more varied content, a finding said to cut against the assumption that mergers narrow coverage. The study is a single preprint, read only through an abstract or excerpt, and its full text was not read; another study in the results points the other way.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that the state protects contracts and otherwise stays out, so a few owners may buy up papers and channels, and news may follow only what sells, with no public broadcaster to cover what the market does not pay for. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Smith, The Wealth of Nations

models.best: Inferred from its principle that prices carry knowledge spread across many people, so what audiences pay for shows what media should carry, and no planner needs to allocate frequencies or papers. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that credit expansion distorts production, so cheap credit funds rival papers and channels that their audiences cannot support, and the bust that follows closes outlets and leaves staff unpaid. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Hayek, The Use of Knowledge in Society

models.best: The case Newspaper ownership concentration and content variety found that greater ownership concentration went with more varied content, a finding said to cut against the assumption that mergers narrow coverage. Inferred from its principle that markets should decide ownership, if the finding holds, deregulation need not narrow coverage. The study is a single preprint read only through an abstract or excerpt, and another study points the other way.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that deregulation and privatisation open media to the market, so a few large owners may buy up outlets, advertisers may set what is printed, and public-interest news may lose its funding as public broadcasting is cut back. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Harvey, A Brief History of Neoliberalism

models.best: The case Public Broadcasting Act of 1967 and federal funding records the Corporation for Public Broadcasting, a private nonprofit, funded by Congress two years ahead through advance appropriations, so its money is planned well in advance. The source is a summary of two editions, not read in full.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that public spending should rise in slumps and fall in booms, so broadcasting budgets are raised and cut for demand reasons rather than for programmes, and outlets' plans swing with the cycle. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Beveridge, Social Insurance and Allied Services

models.best: The FTC case against Meta over Instagram and WhatsApp shows a regulator suing to split a platform, on the FTC's view that the purchases were made to snuff out rising rivals. A 2025 ruling threw the case out, and as of January 2026 the agency was still pushing to revive it; the reports, read only through a summary, leave its status unsettled.
models.worst: Germany's household licence fee and the dispute over its rise shows a rise that the KEF commission sought for 2025 never taking effect, because several states objected. ARD and ZDF filed a constitutional complaint in November 2024 to force it. The sources disagree on whether all 16 states must still approve changes, and they were read through a summary, not in full. Source: European Audiovisual Observatory, IRIS Merlin legal updates (2025 and 2026); The Local, news reports (2010 and 2024)

models.best: The case BBC licence fee and advert-free broadcasting shows a public broadcaster paid by a licence rather than advertising: advertising was ruled out for the early BBC, so listeners paid instead, and from 1927 nearly all licence income went to the BBC. The source is a newspaper history read only through a summary, and no fee amounts are given here.
models.worst: The case NHK household fee upheld as a legal duty describes a broadcaster funded by a fee per household rather than by advertising. In December 2017 the top court upheld the 1950 Broadcast Law and ruled that paying the fee is a legal obligation for anyone who owns a television, and skeptics are reported to doubt that such guaranteed income is justified. The item is a 2017 news report read only through a summary, and reports no current fee or later reform. Source: Advanced Television, news item on the ruling (2017)

models.best: Inferred from its principle that the state directs credit and export targets to chosen industries, so it may back domestic broadcasters and publishers to build national capacity, and it disciplines them by their performance. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that the state picks winners, so favoured papers and channels get credit and shelter from rivals, and firms that stop performing keep that shelter. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Johnson, MITI and the Japanese Miracle

models.best: Inferred from its principle that the rent of land funds public services, so rent on scarce sites used for printing and broadcasting can pay for public media, and holding such sites idle does not pay. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that land values rise without effort by owners, so speculators may hold valuable sites for printing and broadcasting unused, and the gain goes to them rather than to public media. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: George, Progress and Poverty

models.best: Inferred from its principle that cooperative communities built by example replace private profit, so a community can found its own press, school and hall, owned in common and shared by its members. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that planned associations are built by example, so a community press depends on its founders' gifts, and when they withdraw or disagree the paper closes and its readers lose a voice. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Fourier, Le Nouveau Monde industriel

models.best: Inferred from its principle that mutual credit and free contracts let workers keep the full value of their work, so printers and writers can form associations that own their presses and lend to one another at cost. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that free contracts leave small associations without the capital for costly broadcasting, so national reporting may depend on the few who can raise large sums, while small papers stay local. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Proudhon, What Is Property?

models.best: Inferred from its principle that members own and control firms, one member one vote, and share the surplus between users and workers, so a newspaper or broadcaster can be owned together by its readers and staff. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that the surplus is shared between users and workers, so a media co-operative may serve its members' interests above the wider public, and public-interest reporting with no paying members may go unfunded. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Mondragón cooperatives

models.best: Inferred from its principle that goods are shared by need within federated communes, so presses, papers and broadcasting equipment are held in common, and news is free to every member. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that free association replaces contracts, so papers and broadcasts depend on volunteer labour, and reporting that needs paid, sustained work may thin out where volunteers are scarce. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Kropotkin, The Conquest of Bread

models.best: Inferred from its principle that workers' organisations run industry directly, so unions of printers and broadcast staff run their papers and stations, and the people who make the news decide what it contains. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that strikes, and eventually a general strike, are the means of control, so a union that runs a paper may use that power to silence rival voices and bend coverage toward its own disputes. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Pelloutier, Histoire des Bourses du travail

models.best: The case Italy's 1975 reform of the state broadcaster RAI moved oversight from the executive to Parliament and changed RAI's status from state-run to public. One overview, read only through a summary and with no year shown, says RAI became more pluralistic and less censored, though patronage deepened; sources differ on the law's number and date, and the results do not show how that oversight worked in practice.
models.worst: The case NHK household fee upheld as a legal duty raises a concern about a public enterprise whose income is guaranteed by law: NHK is funded by a fee per household rather than by advertising. In December 2017 the top court upheld the 1950 Broadcast Law and ruled that paying the fee is a legal obligation for anyone who owns a television, and skeptics are reported to doubt that such guaranteed income is justified. The item is a 2017 news report read only through a summary, with no current fee or later reform reported. Source: Advanced Television, news item on the ruling (2017)

models.best: Inferred from its principle that workers and consumers share control of industry through guild-like councils, so papers and stations are run by councils of their staff and readers, with the state as one partner among several. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that councils share control among trades, so a guild of journalists or printers may close its ranks, keep outsiders out, and decide among themselves which voices are heard. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Cole, Self-Government in Industry

models.best: Inferred from its principle that state ownership and central plans set output, so public presses and broadcasters are built to central targets for output and reach, with the state owning every outlet. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that a central plan sets output, so papers and programmes are judged by plan targets rather than by readers, and state ownership of every outlet leaves no independent source of news. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Kornai, The Socialist System

models.best: Inferred from its principle that public ownership works with market prices, so public papers and broadcasters are run by managers who respond to what readers and listeners buy, while a central board sets the rules and the investment. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that a central board sets investment, so funds for new outlets and for closing old ones depend on that board's judgement, and managers who follow prices may still lack the capital to start a new paper. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Yugoslav workers' self-management

models.best: Inferred from its principle that after the state withers away and classes disappear, distribution follows need, so presses and broadcasting serve everyone without owners or sales. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that a transition under state power comes first, so a state press may serve the ruling party during that period, and the withering of the state may be put off. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Marx, Critique of the Gotha Programme

models.best: Inferred from its principle that public ownership of key sectors runs beside markets, so some publishers and outlets may compete for readers and advertising while the state keeps the largest broadcasters. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: The case China Media Group and state control of broadcasters describes a March 2018 reform plan to merge state broadcasters into one group, which answers to the Central Propaganda Department of the Chinese Communist Party and is steered by it in practice. The declared aims are tighter domestic thought control and a friendlier image overseas. The source is secondary commentary on the 2018 restructuring, read through a summary, and it shows no later change. Source: China Media Project, article on the 2018 reform (2018); Safeguard Defenders, blog post on the ownership and control of Chinese media (year not shown)

models.best: Inferred from its principle that workers' and consumers' councils plan through repeated proposals, so papers and broadcasts are planned with the people who make and use them, and neither owners nor central planners set the content. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that councils plan through repeated proposals, so decisions on what to publish may take many rounds, and news that needs speed may arrive after the event has passed. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Albert and Hahnel, Looking Forward

models.best: Inferred from its principle that employers and unions are organised into state-controlled bodies, so a broadcaster's board can seat owners, journalists and unions together, with the state setting its national purpose. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: The case Italy's 1975 reform of the state broadcaster RAI describes a secret pact between the Christian Democrats and the Socialists that split control of RAI's two channels, with patronage deepening. This rests on one author's overview, read only through a summary, and sources differ on the law's number and date. Source: Eli Noam, overview of broadcasting in Italy, Columbia Business School (year not shown); other Italian sources in the results for the law details

models.best: Inferred from its principle that finance shares profit and risk, so a publishing or broadcasting venture is funded by partners who share its results, and zakat can fund public-service media without interest-bearing debt. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that interest is prohibited, so media ventures that need large, quick borrowing may find finance scarce, and partners who share the risk may hold back small papers from expanding into national reporting. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Chapra, Towards a Just Monetary System

models.best: Inferred from its principle that economic life serves well-being, so papers and stations stay small, local and non-violent in tone, with moderate consumption and no push to win audiences by sensation. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that production is small-scale and local, so outlets may lack the resources and reach for national reporting, investigative work and broadcasting across regions. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Schumacher, Small Is Beautiful

models.best: Inferred from its principle that widespread private property and small enterprise are the aim, so many small owners run local papers and stations, and decisions stay with the smallest competent body. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that a just wage and small owners are the aim, so large chains that buy up local papers may squeeze out small owners, and national broadcasting may sit with a few large firms beyond local control. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Belloc, The Servile State

models.best: Inferred from its principle that activity stays within planetary limits and everyone has a social floor, so public broadcasting is funded to serve all, and outlets have no growth imperative to push ever higher sales. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that there is no growth imperative, so media may be starved of investment in new outlets and formats, and local papers that need growth to survive may close with no replacement. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Raworth, Doughnut Economics

models.best: Inferred from its principle that every citizen receives an unconditional income, so people can pay for news, books and public-interest media directly, and outlets answer to readers' payments rather than to advertisers. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that the income is unconditional, so people may spend it on whatever they choose, and public-interest news that few people pay for may go unfunded, because nothing ties the money to news. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Van Parijs, Real Freedom for All

models.best: Inferred from its principle that a government which issues its own currency can fund full employment and public services, so public broadcasting and local news need not depend on advertisers, and inflation, not debt, is the limit to watch. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that inflation is the only real limit, so public money for media could be set by ministers rather than by a fixed rule, and outlets might be funded or cut by whoever holds the budget at the time. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Kelton, The Deficit Myth

models.best: Inferred from its principle that communities who share a resource govern it with rules they design, monitor and enforce, so a local radio station, paper or shared platform can be run by its users under rules they set. There is no documented case in the pool.
models.worst: Inferred from its principle that insiders design and enforce the rules, so community media may close its doors to newcomers and favour long-standing members, leaving outsiders no route to air their views. There is no documented case in the pool. Source: Ostrom, Governing the Commons

compromise.summary: Fund public broadcasting from a household fee, set under a fixed rule and kept free of advertising. Give its outlets a multi-party board, and judge media mergers by their measured effect on local news variety. Review the design over five years.
compromise.details: Keeps: advert-free licence funding of Nordic social democracy (BBC licence fee and advert-free broadcasting, a newspaper history); open ownership judged by variety in Classical laissez-faire capitalism and Monetarist neoliberalism (Newspaper ownership concentration and content variety, a single preprint). Blocks: a state objection that froze a rise in the fee (Germany's household licence fee and the dispute over its rise), safeguarded by a rule that the fee rises unless parliament overrides it by a set majority within a fixed time; state steering of news (Mercantilism), safeguarded by a multi-party board with fixed terms and no ministry role in programming. Test: over five years, measure independent ownership of local news outlets, audience reach of public and private news, years between fee decisions and complaints of political interference. Source: Irish News, 'A history of the TV licence fee' (2020); Lisa George, preprint on arXiv (2001); European Audiovisual Observatory, IRIS Merlin legal updates (2025 and 2026); The Local, news reports (2010 and 2024); Heckscher, Mercantilism.
